short_title: Effective Communication under the ISM Code, Engine Resource Management, and Communication Failure
text_verbatim: a) Explain ''Effective communication" as mentioned in the ISM Code. How can principles of Engine Resource Management be used to improve communication on board and with outsiders. Give two examples of near misses or accidents which were mainly due to incorrect, faulty, or unclear communication and how this could have been avoided through assessment or monitoring?

technical_ambiguities: Whether the ISM Code contains a defined term 'effective communication'. It does not define it as a term of art. What it does is impose SPECIFIC COMMUNICATION OBLIGATIONS across several elements - the working language, the ability of personnel to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties, the reporting chain, the master's authority and the designated person link. The answer says so explicitly rather than inventing a definition and attributing it to the Code, and then explains the concept the Code's provisions collectively create.

Whether ERM and BRM are the same thing. The principles are shared - situational awareness, workload management, closed-loop communication, challenge and response, briefing - but the setting differs materially. The engine room has higher noise, more remote and unattended operation, more contractor interface and a different watch structure. The answer notes the shared origin and then writes to the engine room.

Whether 'outsiders' means shore management only. It does not. It means everyone outside the engineering team - shore technical management, the designated person, riding squads and contractors, terminal and port staff, class surveyors and port State officers, tug and pilot during manoeuvring. Answering only 'the office' loses half the demand.

Whether the examples must be real casualties. The stem says 'give two examples' and does not require named cases. Because no casualty report is held, they are constructed illustrations of recognised failure classes and are labelled as such - which is both honest and, for a candidate, safer than half-remembering a real report.

Whether 'assessment or monitoring' is a general phrase or an ISM reference. It is read as pointing at the Code's own machinery - the reporting of non-conformities and near misses, internal audit, the master's review, and management review - because the stem's opening tied the whole question to the Code.

steps.title: What the ISM Code actually says about communication
points: The Code defines no term 'effective communication' - it imposes specific obligations across several elements
Working language established and used; personnel able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties
Reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; the master's authority; the designated person as the direct shore link

steps.title: The concept those provisions create
points: Communication as a managed, documented, auditable process - not a personal skill
The test is whether the message produced the right action, not whether it was sent

steps.title: The principles of Engine Resource Management
points: Situational awareness · workload and task management · closed-loop communication · challenge and response · briefing and debriefing · use of all available resources · decision-making under a flattened authority gradient · error trapping

steps.title: Applying them on board
points: Watch handover, standing and night orders, toolbox talks, permit to work, closed-loop readback for critical operations, UMS and alarm-response protocols

steps.title: Applying them with outsiders
points: Shore technical management and the DPA; riding squads and contractors; terminal and port; class and PSC; bridge, pilot and tugs during manoeuvring

steps.title: Two examples, each with its avoidance analysis
points: Example 1 - an incomplete handover during a changeover
Example 2 - an isolation not confirmed between engine room and contractor
Both are constructed illustrations, and the answer says so

steps.title: The assessment and monitoring machinery that closes the loop
points: Near-miss and non-conformity reporting · internal audit · master's review · management review - the Code's own mechanisms, and why reporting culture is the precondition for all of them

understand_first: Most things that go badly wrong at sea are not caused by somebody not knowing what to do. They are caused by two people each holding half of what was needed and never putting the halves together. One man knows the pump has been isolated; the other knows somebody is about to work on it; neither knows what the other knows. The equipment was adequate, the procedures existed, and the accident happened anyway. The insight behind the safety management regime is that this is not a matter of individual carelessness to be solved by telling people to be careful. It is a systems problem, and it can be engineered against. If information has to pass between people for an operation to be safe, then the passing of that information is itself part of the operation and has to be designed, written down, practised and checked - exactly like a lubricating oil system. That is why a safety management code, which one might expect to be about equipment and procedures, spends so much of its attention on who tells whom, in what language, and with what record. The second idea comes from aviation and was adopted at sea. It was noticed that crashes were happening in aircraft where somebody in the cockpit knew perfectly well that something was wrong and did not say so effectively - or said it, and was not heard, because of who they were and who the captain was. The response was to train crews in a set of specific, teachable habits: say things back to confirm you heard them correctly, brief the team before a critical operation so everybody shares the same picture, and make it normal and safe for a junior person to challenge a senior one. Applied to a machinery space rather than a cockpit, that is what resource management means here. The third idea is the one the question closes on. Because communication is a process, it can be measured. If people report the near misses, if the audits look at handovers and permits rather than only at paperwork, and if management actually reads what comes back, then the failures show up as a pattern before they show up as a casualty.

blocks.h: 1. What the ISM Code actually says about communication

blocks.p: A point of accuracy first, because it earns a mark and prevents a fabrication: the ISM Code does not define 'effective communication' as a term of art. There is no definitions entry for it. What the Code does is impose a series of specific communication obligations, spread across several of its elements, and it is those obligations taken together that create the concept the question is asking about.
The obligations are these:

headers: Why it is a communication requirement
rows: A working language is established and used. The safety management system documentation is in a working language understood by the personnel, and where the working language is not one they understand, translation is provided.

The Code's single most concrete communication provision. It recognises that a multinational crew cannot be assumed to share a language, and it makes the shared language a system requirement rather than a hope.
Personnel are able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties related to the safety management system.
This is the provision the question's phrase comes closest to. The test is functional - not fluency in the abstract, but the ability to do the job safely in the language actually used.

Procedures ensure that new personnel and personnel transferred to new assignments are given proper familiarisation, and that essential instructions are identified, documented and given before sailing.
Familiarisation is a communication process, and the Code makes it a documented one.
Non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences are reported to the Company, investigated and analysed, with corrective action taken.
It obliges information to travel upwards and ashore, which is precisely the direction it does not travel by itself.

The master's responsibility and authority - to implement the safety policy, motivate the crew, issue appropriate orders and instructions in a clear and simple manner, verify that requirements are observed, and review the system and report deficiencies ashore.
The words 'clear and simple manner' are the Code's own, and they are worth quoting because they are the closest it comes to prescribing how to communicate.
The Company designates a person or persons ashore having direct access to the highest level of management, providing a link between the Company and those on board.
It creates a communication channel that bypasses the ordinary commercial chain, so that a safety concern cannot be filtered out by the people it might embarrass.
Documents are available, valid, and obsolete documents promptly removed.
A superseded procedure in circulation is a communication failure waiting to happen.
Drills and exercises for emergency preparedness, with the response organisation described.
Emergency communication has to be practised, because it is the first thing that fails under pressure.

blocks.p: Taken together, the Code treats communication not as a personal attribute but as a managed process which is part of the safety management system, and which is therefore documented, trained, audited and improved like any other part of it.
Four consequences follow, and stating them is what turns a list of Code provisions into an explanation:

ul: Communication is effective when it produces the correct action, not when it has been sent. An instruction that was given, and was not understood, has failed. This is the operative test and it should be stated in those words.

It must work in both directions. The Code obliges information to flow down as orders and up as reports, and it is the upward flow that requires deliberate construction, because it is the one that does not happen naturally.
It must work between ship and shore. The designated person exists precisely so that the channel is not dependent on goodwill.

It must survive the conditions. Noise, alarms, fatigue, an unfamiliar accent over a handheld radio and the pressure of an emergency all degrade it, which is why the Code requires the arrangements to be documented rather than improvised.

blocks.h: 3. The principles of Engine Resource Management

blocks.p: Resource management originated in aviation as crew resource management, was adopted on the bridge as Bridge Resource Management, and is applied in the machinery space as Engine Resource Management. The setting matters: the engine room is noisier, is frequently unattended, involves contractors and riding squads to a degree the bridge does not, and works to a different watch structure. The principles are these:

headers: What it means in a machinery space
rows: Situational awareness

Every member of the team holds an accurate and shared picture of the plant's state - what is running, what is isolated, what is being worked on, and what the ship is about to be asked to do. Most communication failures are a divergence between two people's mental models.
Workload and task management
Recognising overload and redistributing tasks. An overloaded engineer stops communicating first, and that is the warning sign.
Closed-loop communication
The message is sent, read back by the receiver, and the readback confirmed by the sender. Three steps, not one. This alone eliminates a large class of failures.
Challenge and response
Any team member may question an instruction or an observation, and there is an agreed way of escalating if the concern is not resolved. It must be legitimate to challenge, or it will not happen.
Flattening the authority gradient
A junior engineer or a rating must be able to say that something looks wrong to the chief. Where the gradient is too steep the information exists on board and never arrives.
Briefing and debriefing
Before a critical operation the team is briefed on the plan, the hazards, each person's role and the abort criteria; afterwards it is debriefed on what actually happened.
Use of all available resources

People, manuals, alarms, trend data, the makers' service line, class, shore technical support. An engineer struggling alone with a problem when shore expertise is a phone call away is not managing his resources.
Error trapping
Designing the operation so that a single mistake is caught before it has an effect - independent verification, cross-checking, a second signature on an isolation.
Decision-making and standard phraseology
An agreed structure for making and communicating decisions, and agreed words for critical items, so that meaning does not depend on the individual.

ul: Watch handover. A structured, documented handover against a checklist covering plant status, defects, work in progress, isolations and permits open, and anything expected during the coming watch - with the incoming engineer confirming understanding rather than merely signing. This is the highest-value single application of ERM in the engine room.
Standing orders and night orders. Written, specific, and acknowledged, so that the chief engineer's expectations are not a matter of interpretation at three in the morning.
Toolbox talks before a task. The briefing principle applied at working level - the plan, the hazards, who does what, what would make us stop.

Permit to work and isolation control. The formal, signed embodiment of closed-loop communication and error trapping: the isolation is made, verified independently, tagged, and the permit is not issued until both are confirmed. Nothing else in the engine room depends so completely on communication being right.
Closed-loop readback for critical operations. Blackout recovery, changeover of fuels, main engine manoeuvring, tank transfers and bunkering. Orders and confirmations repeated back verbatim.

UMS and alarm response protocols. Under unmanned machinery space operation the duty engineer may be alone and asleep when an alarm sounds. Who is called, by whom, and what is expected of them must be agreed in advance, because it will not be negotiated at the time.
Bunkering and cargo operations. Agreed signals, an agreed shutdown procedure, continuous communication maintained, and a means of stopping the operation immediately available to both ends.

Familiarisation of new joiners. The Code requires it and ERM explains why it matters: a new joiner's mental model of the plant is empty, and every assumption an experienced engineer makes about shared knowledge is false.
Debriefing after drills and after incidents. Where the learning actually happens, and the step most often skipped.

blocks.p: The stem asks about communication with outsiders as well as on board, and this half of the demand is frequently dropped. 'Outsiders' means everyone outside the engineering team:

headers: The communication that matters, and the ERM principle behind it
rows: Shore technical management

Defect reporting, spares, technical advice, and agreement on repair strategy. Use of all available resources - the ship should not solve alone what the office can help with. Reports must be factual and complete, because the office cannot see the plant.
The designated person ashore

The Code's dedicated safety channel with direct access to the highest level of management. Its whole purpose is to flatten the authority gradient between ship and Company, so that a safety concern is not filtered by commercial pressure. Every seafarer must know who the DPA is and how to reach them.
Riding squads and contractors

The single highest-risk interface in the engine room. They may not share the working language, will not know the ship's systems, and are not in the ship's watch structure. Requires induction, a permit-to-work regime that binds them, a named ship's officer responsible for them, and explicit isolation confirmation. Error trapping and closed-loop communication, formally applied.
Terminal and port
Bunkering and cargo interfaces - agreed signals, agreed rates and shutdown procedure, a common language, and an emergency stop available to both parties.
Bridge, pilot and tugs during manoeuvring

The engine room must know what the bridge intends before it is ordered. A pre-arrival briefing between master and chief engineer, covering expected manoeuvring, machinery limitations, power availability and any restrictions, is briefing and shared situational awareness across two teams - and its absence is a classic cause of engine failure at the worst moment.
Class surveyors and port State control officers
Accurate, unevasive presentation of condition, records and defects. Attempting to conceal a defect is a communication failure with regulatory consequences.
Makers' service engineers
Precise symptom description and accurate data - a technical communication in which imprecision leads directly to the wrong part being flown out.

blocks.h: 6. Two examples of occurrences caused mainly by communication failure

blocks.p: These two scenarios are constructed illustrations of recognised failure classes, not accounts of named casualties. They are given in that form deliberately, and a candidate should present them the same way rather than half-recalling a real investigation report.
Example 1 — an incomplete watch handover leading to loss of lubricating oil pressure.

ul: What happened. During a watch, the duty engineer changed over the main engine lubricating oil filters and left the standby filter isolated pending cleaning of the element. The handover to the oncoming watch was verbal, hurried and taken in the machinery control room during a meal relief. The isolation was mentioned but not recorded and not confirmed. Later in the oncoming watch the running filter differential rose; the engineer attempted the routine changeover to the standby, which was still isolated, and lubricating oil pressure fell to the low-pressure alarm. The engine slowed down automatically and the ship was briefly without propulsion in coastal waters.

The communication failure. A change to the plant's configuration existed in one engineer's head and nowhere else. The two men's mental models of the system diverged - a failure of shared situational awareness created by an unstructured handover with no readback and no record.

How assessment or monitoring would have caught it. A documented handover checklist with an explicit line for isolations and work in progress, requiring the incoming engineer to confirm rather than sign, converts the omission into a required entry. Tagging of the isolated valve makes the configuration visible without depending on memory. And internal audit of handover records - actually sampling them rather than confirming that the form exists - would have shown handovers being completed with the isolation field blank, which is the pattern that precedes this event.

blocks.p: Example 2 — an isolation not confirmed between ship's staff and a riding squad.

ul: What happened. A riding squad was engaged to renew a section of sea water pipework during a coastal passage. The permit to work was raised and the relevant pump was stopped, but the electrical isolation was requested by the squad's supervisor over a handheld radio in a language not fluently shared, and the ship's engineer understood a different pump to be the subject. The requested pump was stopped; the pump actually connected to the pipework being opened was not isolated and was on automatic standby. It started on a falling-pressure signal while the line was open, and a member of the squad was struck by the discharge. On the facts as constructed, the outcome was a near miss with minor injury; the same failure with a different fluid or a different pressure would not have been.

The communication failure. A critical instruction crossed a language boundary and an organisational boundary with no readback, no independent verification and no shared identification convention for the equipment. Neither party was careless; each was confident, and they were confident about different pumps.

How assessment or monitoring would have caught it. A permit-to-work system that binds contractors and requires the isolation to be physically verified and tagged by a named ship's officer, with the permit signed by both parties at the machine, removes the radio from the critical path altogether. Contractor induction covering the working language, the identification convention for machinery and the stop-work authority addresses the language boundary. Closed-loop readback with the equipment's unique identification repeated back traps the ambiguity. And monitoring: near-miss reporting of earlier occasions when equipment was misidentified over the radio - which almost certainly happened harmlessly before - would have flagged the hazard, and an audit of contractor permits would have shown isolations being recorded without independent verification.

blocks.p: The common feature of both, and worth stating as the analytical point: in neither case was anybody ignorant or negligent. In both cases the information required existed on board and did not reach the person who needed it in a form they acted on correctly. That is what distinguishes a communication failure from a competence failure, and it is why the remedy is a system remedy.

blocks.h: 7. The assessment and monitoring machinery that closes the loop

blocks.p: The stem's closing words - 'through assessment or monitoring' - point back at the Code's own mechanisms, and the answer should finish there:

ul: Reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences. The Code requires them to be reported, investigated and analysed with corrective action. Near-miss reporting is the most valuable safety data a ship produces, because near misses are numerous, free, and share their causes with the accidents that have not happened yet.

A reporting culture is the precondition for everything else. The Code can require reports; only the Company can make it safe to submit them. Where reporting is punished, the mechanism produces silence and management concludes, wrongly, that nothing is going wrong.

Internal audit. Audits must examine whether communication processes are actually working - sampling handover records, permits and isolations - rather than confirming that the forms exist. An audit that verifies the existence of a procedure has assessed nothing.

The master's review. The master's periodic review of the system and reporting of its deficiencies to shore management is a designed upward channel and should be used for exactly this class of finding.

Management review. The Company evaluates the effectiveness of the system. Trends in near misses, repeated non-conformities in the same area, and audit findings on handovers and permits are the evidence that communication is failing before an accident demonstrates it.

Risk assessment. Where a task is identified as depending on communication across a boundary - a contractor, a language, a watch change - the assessment should identify that dependence as a hazard in its own right and control it, which is precisely what a permit-to-work regime does.
Training, drills and debriefs. ERM training, and the deliberate debriefing of drills and incidents, are how the principles at section 3 become habits rather than knowledge.

blocks.p: The closing observation: the Code treats communication as an auditable process precisely so that its failures can be detected by monitoring rather than by casualty. That is the connection between the beginning and the end of this question.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores - and the printed anomaly to notice

blocks.p: The question prints a limb a) and then no b). That is a misprint on the source paper, not a missing question, and it is worth noticing because it means the whole question is one limb containing three separate instructions run together: explain effective communication under the Code, apply ERM on board and with outsiders, and give two worked examples with their avoidance analysis.

As with the salvage question on this paper, the absence of lettering is the hazard. There is nothing to count against, and the commonest failure is a long, comfortable essay on the importance of communication that never reaches the examples - which are worth roughly a third of the marks. Number the three demands in the margin before writing.

blocks.h: Say honestly that the Code defines no such term

blocks.p: The stem says 'as mentioned in the ISM Code', and a candidate naturally starts hunting for a definition. There is none. Saying so is a mark, not an admission. What the Code does is impose communication obligations across several elements, and the concept is what those obligations collectively create.

The provisions to have ready: the working language requirement; that personnel must be able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties; familiarisation of new and transferred personnel; reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; the master's duty to issue orders 'in a clear and simple manner'; the designated person ashore; document control; and drills.

The designated person is the one to develop if time is short. Its purpose is structural: it creates a safety channel with direct access to the highest level of management, deliberately bypassing the ordinary commercial chain, so that a concern cannot be filtered out by the people it might embarrass. That is a communication design decision and explaining it shows the Code has been understood.

blocks.h: The definition of 'effective' worth committing to memory

blocks.p: Communication is effective when it produces the correct action - not when it has been sent. An order given and not understood has failed, and the failure belongs to the system, not to the listener. One sentence, and it frames the whole answer.

blocks.h: ERM is not BRM, and it is not 'talk more'

blocks.p: The stem says Engine Resource Management. The principles are shared with the bridge - both descend from crew resource management in aviation - but write to the machinery space: higher noise, unattended operation, contractors and riding squads, a different watch structure, and an interface with a bridge team that does not see the plant.

And give the principles as named principles, not as encouragement. Situational awareness; workload and task management; closed-loop communication; challenge and response; flattening the authority gradient; briefing and debriefing; use of all available resources; error trapping; standard phraseology. A list of nine named principles is examinable; 'engineers should communicate well' is not.

blocks.h: Closed-loop communication - explain the three steps

blocks.p: It is the single most transferable technique in the answer and most candidates state it in half a line. It has three steps: the sender gives the message; the receiver reads it back; the sender confirms the readback is correct. Only the third step closes the loop. Skipping it leaves the sender assuming, which is exactly the state that produces both examples below.

Half the second demand, and routinely lost. Outsiders are not just the office. The list: shore technical management; the DPA; riding squads and contractors; terminal and port during bunkering and cargo; bridge, pilot and tugs during manoeuvring; class surveyors and PSC officers; makers' service engineers.

Two deserve development. Contractors and riding squads are the highest-risk interface in the engine room, because they combine an unfamiliar language, no knowledge of the ship's systems, and no place in the watch structure. And the pre-arrival briefing between master and chief engineer is shared situational awareness across two teams - the engine room needs to know what the bridge intends before it is ordered, and its absence is a classic cause of machinery failure at the worst possible moment.

blocks.h: The examples - construct them, and say that you have

blocks.p: The stem asks for two examples and does not require named casualties. Constructing a clear scenario is safer and scores better than half-remembering a real investigation report, where a misremembered detail is worse than no detail. Say in the answer that the scenarios are illustrative.

Choose failure classes that are recognisable and different from each other. A handover omission and a cross-boundary isolation failure work well because one is internal and one involves outsiders, which lets both halves of the second demand pay off in the examples.

Structure each example in three parts: what happened; where precisely the communication failed; and what assessment or monitoring would have caught it. The third part is not optional - the stem asks for it explicitly - and it is the part candidates omit.

blocks.h: The analytical point that lifts the answer

blocks.p: In a genuine communication failure nobody is ignorant and nobody is careless. The information needed existed on board and did not reach the person who needed it in a form they acted on correctly. Two competent people were each confident, and confident about different things. Stating that distinguishes a communication failure from a competence failure and explains why the remedy has to be systemic.

blocks.h: Close where the question closes - assessment and monitoring

blocks.p: The stem's final words point at the Code's machinery: near-miss and non-conformity reporting, internal audit, the master's review, and management review. Two observations are worth making rather than just listing them:

ul: Reporting culture is the precondition. The Code can require reports; only the Company can make it safe to submit them. Where reporting is punished the mechanism produces silence, and management concludes that nothing is going wrong.

An audit that confirms a procedure exists has assessed nothing. It must sample the handover records, the permits and the isolations to see whether the process actually operated. That distinction is what makes monitoring capable of catching either of the examples before it happened.
Do not invent a Code definition of 'effective communication'. There is none - say so.
Do not cite a named real casualty or attribute an account to an investigation report.
Do not name an ERM or BRM training course, provider or syllabus.
Do not write general communication theory - sender, channel, receiver, noise. The stem ties the answer to the Code.
Do not omit the two examples or their avoidance analysis. They carry roughly a third of the marks.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Printed as a lone 'a)' with no 'b)' - but THREE instructions. Concept = communication is a managed, documented, auditable process. Test = did it produce the correct action. (2) ERM principles: situational awareness · workload management · closed-loop (send-readback-CONFIRM, three steps) · challenge and response · flatten the authority gradient · briefing and debriefing · use all available resources · error trapping · standard phraseology. ON BOARD: handover checklist, night orders, toolbox talk, permit to work and isolation control, readback for blackout/fuel changeover/manoeuvring/bunkering, UMS alarm protocol, familiarisation, debrief. OUTSIDERS: shore management, DPA, riding squads and contractors (highest-risk interface), terminal, master-chief pre-arrival briefing, class and PSC, makers. (3) TWO examples - incomplete handover → isolated standby LO filter → LO pressure loss; unconfirmed isolation across a language boundary with a contractor → pump auto-starts on an open line. Each closed with: handover checklist and tagging, permit binding contractors, readback with unique equipment ID, near-miss reporting, audit that SAMPLES records. Close on reporting · internal audit · master's review · management review, and say reporting culture is the precondition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the ISM Code define 'effective communication'?

The concept is what those collectively create.

regulations: International Safety Management (ISM) Code, as amended through MSC.353(92) - the edition operative at this sitting. Held in the corpus at true-source/03-imo-instruments/ISM-Code/.

ISM Code - the requirement that the Company establishes and uses a working language, that the safety management system documentation is in a language understood by personnel, and that translation is provided where it is not.

ISM Code - the requirement that personnel are able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties related to the safety management system. This is the provision closest to the phrase the stem uses.
ISM Code - familiarisation of new personnel and personnel transferred to new assignments, and the identification and documentation of essential instructions before sailing.
ISM Code - reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences to the Company, with investigation, analysis and corrective action.

ISM Code - the master's responsibility and authority, including the duty to issue appropriate orders and instructions IN A CLEAR AND SIMPLE MANNER, to verify that specified requirements are observed, and to review the safety management system and report its deficiencies to shore-based management.
ISM Code - the designation of a person or persons ashore having DIRECT ACCESS TO THE HIGHEST LEVEL OF MANAGEMENT, providing a link between the Company and those on board.
ISM Code - document control, including the prompt removal of obsolete documents.
ISM Code - emergency preparedness, the response organisation, and drills and exercises.
ISM Code - internal safety audits, the review of the safety management system, and the Company's evaluation of its effectiveness.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the Indian statute in force at this sitting giving effect to the ISM Code. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and is thirty-seven months future.
